554.title: Why do we hate?
554.hook: Sakka, king of the gods, asks why beings who wish to live without hate still live in hate
554.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the chain in Sakka's questions to show how conflict starts in the mind, and in Theravada countries Sakka is a familiar figure in temple art and stories as a devoted protector of the teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: anicca, and a jeweled city gone back to thatch. Your line: it was grand once, and it's gone. Today, a king of the gods arrives with a musician and a question.
screen: `IT WAS GRAND ONCE, AND IT'S GONE.`

segments.voice: Before the question, a love song. Sakka, king of the gods, wants to see the Buddha, who is sitting in a cave in the hills near Rajagaha. He doesn't just walk in. He sends ahead a celestial musician, Pancasikha, with a lute. Pancasikha stands near the cave and sings a song that mixes praise of the Buddha with longing for a girl he loves. The Buddha listens, and then tells him, kindly: the strings and your voice blend well. Then Sakka comes in, and asks his question.
screen: `A LOVE SONG OUTSIDE A CAVE.` → `THE STRINGS AND VOICE BLEND WELL.` → `THE KING OF THE GODS ASKS.`

segments.voice: The Sakkapanha, Sakka's questions, is the twenty-first Long Discourse. The first question goes like this. Gods, humans, and every other kind of being all wish to live without hate, without violence, without enemies, without ill will. And yet they live in hate, with violence, with enemies. Why? Look at the shape of it. Not, why are other people hateful? Everyone wants peace. Everyone ends up in conflict anyway. What's tying them? The Buddha answers: envy and stinginess. Envy, at what someone else has. Stinginess, about what you have. Sakka is pleased, and asks the obvious next question: and where do those come from? From what we hold dear and what we don't. And that? From desire, wanting. And desire? From thinking, the mind turning something over. And thinking? From what the sutta calls the spreading of perception: the mind taking one small thing and running with it, building a story, then another story on top. Each answer goes one layer down, like peeling a root. And it ends somewhere surprisingly ordinary. In this answer, hate between nations and hate between neighbors start in the same place: a mind that proliferates. Read that way, the answer is both bleak and hopeful. Bleak, because the root is in every mind. Hopeful, because it sits in a place anyone can watch. Sakka says, as each answer lands: so it is, Blessed One. My doubt is cut off.
screen: `EVERYONE WANTS PEACE. WHY NOT?` · `ENVY AND STINGINESS.` · `DEAR, DESIRE, THINKING.` · `THE MIND THAT SPREADS.` · then, large: `WHY DO WE HATE?`

segments.voice: Ask one honest question about yourself, not about anyone else: who do I resent right now, and what do I want that they have? Or: what am I holding tightly? Ask it, breathe, and see if the answer goes one layer deeper on its own; if the mind starts building a story, notice the building.
Issa-macchariya. Sakka's first question in DN 21; the Buddha answers envy and stinginess, rooted in what we hold dear, desire, and the spreading mind. Today's word.
Your line: one layer down. Envy and stinginess, and under them, a mind that spreads. Go gently.

555.title: The great foundations
555.hook: the long satipatthana, with the four truths expanded
555.howItsDone: In Myanmar, Sri Lanka and Thailand the Mahasatipatthana Sutta is often chanted in full, sometimes at the bedside of the dying, and a number of modern meditation methods trace themselves to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: issa-macchariya, envy and stinginess. Your line: one layer down. Today, the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness, in its longer form.

Open the Pali canon in two places and you find nearly the same teaching twice. The teaching on the four foundations of mindfulness has one home in the Middle-Length Discourses, and this path met it there. It has another here, in the twenty-second Long Discourse. For long stretches the two read alike. Then the long one keeps going where the short one moves on, and it's longer for one reason.
screen: `THE SAME TEACHING, TWICE.` → `TWO VERSIONS IN THE CANON.` → `ONE IS LONGER. WHY?`

segments.voice: It's the Mahasatipatthana Sutta, the great discourse on the foundations of mindfulness. It opens among the Kurus with a bold line: this is the direct path for the purification of beings, for overcoming sorrow and lament, for the ending of pain and grief, for realizing nibbana. Namely, the four foundations. Then the four, as before. Body: the breath, the postures, clear awareness in every action, the parts of the body, the elements, the charnel ground. Feelings: pleasant, painful, neither. Mind: with greed or without, with hate or without. And mental qualities: the hindrances, the heaps, the senses, the factors of awakening, and the four noble truths. And here the long version slows right down. What is the truth of suffering? Birth, aging, death, sorrow, lament, pain, grief, despair, and each word is defined. Where does craving arise? Wherever something in the world seems pleasant and agreeable: the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, the mind, and then sights, sounds, smells, contacts, feelings, thoughts, one by one. Where does it cease? In exactly the same places. That repetition is the point. The long way doesn't add new ideas. It walks the same ground slowly enough that you can see craving start and stop in the most ordinary places. And at the end, a promise that shrinks. Whoever practices these four for seven years can expect a fruit. Never mind seven years: six, five, four, all the way down. Never mind a year: seven months, down to half a month. Never mind that: seven days.
screen: `THE DIRECT PATH, AMONG THE KURUS.` · `BODY, FEELING, MIND, QUALITIES.` · `THE FOUR TRUTHS, SLOWED RIGHT DOWN.` · `SEVEN YEARS, DOWN TO SEVEN DAYS.` · then, large: `THE LONG WAY.`

segments.voice: Walk the four foundations once, slowly: feel the body sitting and the breath moving; ask whether this moment is pleasant, unpleasant or neither; then whether the mind is calm or restless, wanting or not; then whether a hindrance is here, or something like interest or ease. Then back to the body, and around again. If you have time, keep going, up to fifteen minutes.
Satipatthana. The Mahasatipatthana Sutta: the four foundations of mindfulness, with the four noble truths unfolded step by step. Today's word.
Your line: the long way. The same ground, walked slowly enough to see. That's day five hundred fifty-five.

fork.reveal: seven years, then six, five, down to one; then seven months; and at last, seven days.

original.note: Pali satipatthana: sati, mindfulness; patthana or upatthana, foundation or establishing.

trapdoor: what you thought: the long and short versions of the sutta teach different things.
what it means: they teach the same four foundations; the long one walks through the four truths in detail.
what a scholar hears: DN 22 is MN 10 plus an expanded saccapabba; whether satipatthana means 'foundation' (patthana) or 'establishing' (upatthana) of mindfulness is debated.
recall: a great reference for checking teaching

chat.says: Why is there a long version of the mindfulness discourse? Does it teach something new?
options: Not really: it walks the four truths slowly, so you see craving start and stop.
Yes, it adds secret practices that the shorter discourse leaves out entirely.
It's longer because it's meant only for monks who practice for seven years.
chat.meaning: The long version walks the same four foundations, but unfolds the four noble truths word by word, showing where craving arises and where it ceases.

556.title: The sceptic's parables
556.hook: Prince Payasi argues against rebirth; Kumara Kassapa answers with stories
556.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often retell the parables of the Payasi Sutta, especially the hemp carrier, when talking about holding views, and many traditions treat honest doubt as a question to explore rather than a fault.

segments.voice: Yesterday: satipatthana, the four foundations walked the long way. Your line: the long way. Today, a long argument, and nobody in it is a villain.

Payasi is a ruler of the town of Setavya, and he has a firm view. There is no world after this one. No beings reborn. No fruit of good or bad deeds. And he's not lazy about it. He's tested it. He's asked dying friends who lived badly to come back and warn him, if there's anything after. None came. He's asked dying friends who lived well to come back and tell him. None came. So he concludes: nothing. When a monk named Kumara Kassapa comes through, Payasi goes out to argue.
screen: `NO WORLD BEYOND, SAYS PAYASI.` → `HE ASKED THE DYING TO RETURN.` → `NONE CAME.`

segments.voice: The Payasi Sutta, the twenty-third Long Discourse, is set after the Buddha's death, and it's almost all stories. To the first experiment, Kassapa answers with a thief. A man is caught, and on the way to execution he says: let me go home first, just to say goodbye. Would the guards let him? No. Then why expect someone in a hard rebirth to be allowed back to report? To the second, a man who has fallen into a pit of filth. He's pulled out, scrubbed, perfumed, dressed in fine clothes. Would he want to go back down into the pit? No. Then why expect someone in a happy world to come back here? Payasi tries harder experiments, and Kassapa answers with more stories. A village hears a conch for the first time and asks the shell to speak again, but it only sounds when someone blows it with effort. And at last, when Payasi says that even so, he can't give up a view he's known for, Kassapa tells one more. Two friends find a bundle of hemp. Later they find hemp thread, then cloth, then silver, then gold. One friend swaps up each time. The other says: no, I've carried this hemp a long way, and it's well tied. And he walks home with the hemp. Look at how Kassapa argues. He never mocks. He treats Payasi's doubt as a real question that deserves a real answer, and answers it with pictures anyone can weigh. Whether you find the answers convincing is yours to decide. The sutta's respect for the question is plain.
screen: `A THIEF ON THE WAY TO EXECUTION.` · `A MAN PULLED FROM THE PIT.` · `THE SHELL THAT WON'T SPEAK ALONE.` · `THE MAN WHO KEPT HIS HEMP.` · then, large: `THE SCEPTIC'S PARABLES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one doubt you hold, about a teaching, about yourself, about anything, and treat it the way Kassapa treated Payasi: as a fair question from someone worth talking to. Breathe with it, then check gently: am I keeping this view because I've weighed it, or because I've carried it a long way? Either answer is fine.
Upama. In DN 23 Kumara Kassapa answers Payasi's doubts about rebirth with stories, never with scorn. Today's word.
Your line: a picture, not a put-down. Kassapa never mocks; he simply answers. Until tomorrow.

557.title: Your own pasture
557.hook: be islands to yourselves; keep to your own ancestral pasture
557.carry: come back to your own ground
557.howItsDone: Buddhist meditation teachers often describe the four foundations of mindfulness as the practitioner's home ground, and the hawk-and-quail story is a familiar teaching picture in many Theravada communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday: upama, Kassapa's parables. Your line: a picture, not a put-down. Today a three-day discourse begins, close to home.

A quail is pecking in open country, far from home, when a hawk drops out of the sky and grabs it. As it's carried off, the quail laments: if only I'd stayed on my own ground, the ground of my fathers, you'd never have caught me. And where's that? asks the hawk. A plowed field, full of clods. The hawk, sure of its own strength, lets it go: back you go, then; you won't escape me even there. The quail flies to a big clod, stands on top, and calls out a dare. The hawk dives. At the last moment the quail slips into a crack in the clod, and the hawk slams breast-first into the earth.
screen: `A QUAIL IN THE OPEN.` → `IF ONLY I'D STAYED HOME.` → `THE HAWK HITS THE CLOD.`

segments.voice: That quail story comes from the Connected Discourses, and it brings to life the image that opens the twenty-sixth Long Discourse, the Cakkavatti Sihanada, the lion's roar on the wheel-turning king. The Buddha is at Matula in Magadha, and he begins: monks, live as islands to yourselves, as your own refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as your island, the Dhamma as your refuge. Then the image itself: keep to your own pasture, the range of your fathers. Walking there, Mara, the tempter, will get no chance at you. The Pali for pasture is gocara: range, the ground an animal knows and feeds on. And what is a monk's own pasture? The Buddha says it plainly: the four foundations of mindfulness. Body, feeling, mind, and mental qualities. That's home ground. This doesn't mean stay in your bubble, or never go out. The quail isn't safe because it hides. It's safe because it's somewhere it knows well, where it has cover. The open country, the Connected Discourses say, is the pull of the five senses. Out there, scrolling and comparing and chasing, the hawk can dive. Back on familiar ground, with attention resting on the breath, the body, what's actually happening, the hawk can't get a grip. The discourse goes on into a long story about kings and the human future. But it starts with a bird finding its way home.
screen: `THE QUAIL AND THE HAWK.` · `ISLANDS TO YOURSELVES.` · `GOCARA: THE GROUND YOU KNOW.` · `HOME GROUND: THE FOUR FOUNDATIONS.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN PASTURE.`

segments.voice: Come back to your own ground: feel the body sitting, one clod in the field; feel the breath, another; notice whether this moment is pleasant or not, another. When the mind wanders out into the open, into plans or worries or other people's lives, notice the hawk's shadow and step back behind the clod.
Gocara. In DN 26 the Buddha says: keep to your own ground, the four foundations of mindfulness, and the tempter gets no chance. Today's word.
Your line: come back to your own ground. Home ground is where the hawk can't get a grip. Day five hundred fifty-seven, done.

Yes: stay in your bubble and avoid anyone who thinks differently from you.

558.title: Poverty breeds violence
558.hook: a king neglects the poor; theft, then weapons, then killing follow
558.howItsDone: Buddhist social thinkers in Asia and beyond often cite the Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta when they speak about poverty and crime, and many Buddhist communities run food banks, clinics and relief work.

segments.voice: Yesterday: gocara, the quail and the hawk. Your line: come back to your own ground. Today the same discourse leaves the field and walks into a palace.

In the old story there are wheel-turning kings, rulers so just that a great jeweled wheel appears in the sky and rolls ahead of them, and other kingdoms simply welcome them. The first, Dalhanemi, grows old, hands the throne to his son, and goes forth. The wheel vanishes. The son asks his father what to do, and is told: the wheel isn't an inheritance. You have to earn it. Rule by the Dhamma. Protect everyone, even the birds and beasts. And give wealth to those who have none. Generations later, a king forgets that last part.
screen: `A WHEEL IN THE SKY.` → `NOT AN INHERITANCE.` → `ONE KING FORGETS.`

segments.voice: This king, in the Cakkavatti Sihanada, rules by his own ideas. He protects people, but he doesn't give wealth to the needy. And so, the text says, poverty spreads. Then a man steals. He's caught and brought before the king. Why did you steal? Because I had nothing to live on, sire. So the king gives him money: live on this, support your parents, your wife and children, start a business, give to holy people. Good. But word gets around, and others steal, hoping for the same. Now the king panics. If I keep giving money to thieves, theft will only grow. So he does the opposite: he has the next thief bound, paraded through the streets to the beat of a harsh drum, and beheaded. And what happens? People hear, and think: then we'll carry sharp swords, and kill those we rob so nobody can report us. Theft becomes killing. Then lying, to cover it. Then slander, and on down a long list, and with every step, human life gets shorter and uglier. Look at the chain the sutta draws. The trouble doesn't start with a wicked thief. It starts with a king who didn't share. Then a harsh answer to a symptom makes it worse. It's an old Indian story, and the Buddha tells it as a story, with fantastic numbers and ages. But the chain it draws doesn't need the fantastic numbers: when people have nothing, and the only answer is punishment, the text says violence grows.
screen: `HE DIDN'T GIVE TO THE NEEDY.` · `THE FIRST THIEF IS HELPED.` · `THE NEXT ONE IS BEHEADED.` · `THEN EVERYONE CARRIES A SWORD.` · then, large: `POVERTY BREEDS VIOLENCE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who doesn't have enough, a person you pass on the street, a family you've heard about, and let their situation be real for a moment, not an idea. Breathe with it, then let one small, concrete thing come to mind that you could give: money, food, time, a phone call. You don't have to decide yet; just let it be clear.

Your line: give something real, however small. The trouble began with a king who didn't share. See you tomorrow.

559.title: People turn again
559.hook: human life shrinks, then people turn back to goodness; Metteyya will come
559.carry: glad to see each other alive
559.howItsDone: Buddhist traditions across Asia honor Metteyya, or Maitreya, as the coming Buddha, sometimes shown seated with feet on the ground, ready to rise, and some Buddhists make merit in the hope of meeting his teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a king who stopped sharing, and the violence that followed. Your line: give something real, however small. Today the same story hits bottom, and then something turns.

The Cakkavatti Sihanada keeps going down. With every new kind of wrongdoing, the story says, human lifespans shrink, from tens of thousands of years down to just ten. Fine foods disappear. Even the idea of a good deed disappears; there's not even a word for good. People treat each other like animals. Then comes what the text calls a sword-interval: seven days in which people see each other as prey, and kill. It's a dark page. It isn't the end.
screen: `LIFE SHRINKS TO TEN YEARS.` → `NO WORD FOR GOOD.` → `SEVEN DAYS OF SWORDS.`

segments.voice: During those seven days, some people slip away. They hide in long grass, in thickets, in forests, among rocks and rivers, living on roots and fruit. When the seven days are over, they come out, see each other, and embrace. The story gives their words simply: how good to see living beings still alive! Then they talk. We lost so much because we took up wrong ways. What if we gave up just one thing? What if we stopped killing? And they do. Just that one. Their children live longer than they did. Seeing this, they give up something else: taking what isn't given. Then sexual misconduct. Then lying, slander, harsh speech, and on down the list. Each generation adds one good thing, and human life lengthens again, all the way back to eighty thousand years. Then, the Buddha says, a Buddha named Metteyya will arise in the world, as I have arisen now. He will teach the same Dhamma, good in the beginning, the middle and the end, and lead a community of many thousands, as I lead hundreds. Two things stand out. The turn starts with one small change, made by frightened people who are simply glad to see each other alive. Not a hero, not a king. And the hope is long. Under his Sanskrit name, Maitreya, the Buddha to come is honored in lands far from where this was first told. Some readers hear in the name Metteyya the word metta, loving-kindness. After all that darkness, the future has a kind name.
screen: `THE ONES WHO HID.` · `HOW GOOD TO SEE YOU ALIVE.` · `ONE GOOD THING AT A TIME.` · `METTEYYA WILL COME.` · then, large: `PEOPLE TURN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Let the picture of the survivors come: people stepping out of the forest, seeing each other, glad, and breathe with that gladness. Then look forward with hope rather than worry, and picture one good change that could spread, one generation adding one thing, maybe one you could start. Rest with that future for a while.

560.title: They tasted the earth
560.hook: beings of light taste the earth's savory crust and grow coarse
560.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers retell the Agganna Sutta as a story about craving and pride rather than a scientific account, and mindful eating, with attention to each bite, is practiced in many Buddhist monasteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday: survivors stepping out of the forest. Your line: glad to see each other alive. Today a week closes with a very old story about the first bite.

Two young men, Vasettha and Bharadvaja, were born brahmins and are training to become monks. Other brahmins revile them for it. Brahmins, they say, are the highest class, born from Brahma's own mouth. The Buddha answers dryly: brahmin women are seen pregnant and giving birth, just like everyone else. Born from Brahma's mouth? Then he tells them a story of how things began. It's the twenty-seventh Long Discourse, the Agganna, the discourse on beginnings.
screen: `TWO BRAHMINS BECOMING MONKS.` → `BORN FROM BRAHMA'S MOUTH?` → `A STORY OF BEGINNINGS.`

segments.voice: There comes a time, the story goes, when the world rolls up and comes apart, and beings are reborn in a realm of radiance. They're made of mind, feed on joy, shine with their own light, and move through the air. Then the world rolls out again, all water and darkness, no sun, no moon, and the beings come back to it. Over the water spreads a savory earth, like the skin that forms on hot milk as it cools. It has the color of fine ghee and tastes like pure honey. Then one being, of a greedy nature, the text says, wonders what this can be, and tastes it with a finger. Delicious. Craving comes. Others copy him, and soon they're breaking off lumps with their hands. As they eat, their own light fades. Then the sun and moon appear, night and day, the seasons. Their bodies grow coarse. Some look better than others, and the better-looking ones grow proud. With that pride, the savory earth vanishes. They gather and lament: oh, the taste! The story goes on, step by step, through coarser foods. Look at what drives it. Not a curse, not a punishment from above. Just tasting, wanting more, comparing, pride. Some readers hear gentle humor here too, a story built to answer the brahmins' claims. And the week behind us: why do we hate, the great foundations, the skeptic's parables, your own pasture, poverty breeds violence, people turn again, and now beings of light, licking a finger.
screen: `BEINGS OF LIGHT, FEEDING ON JOY.` · `A SAVORY SKIN ON THE WATER.` · `ONE TASTE, THEN HANDFULS.` · `THE LIGHT FADES, PRIDE GROWS.` · then, large: `THEY TASTED THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: If you have something small to eat nearby, a raisin, a piece of bread, a sip of tea, look at it and smell it, then take the smallest bite and let it sit on the tongue. Notice the first flavor, and then the wanting that comes right after: more. Don't fight it; just see it arrive, like the first being with the finger, and if there's nothing to eat, do this with a breath.
rasapathavi. In DN 27 shining beings taste the savory crust of the new world; craving and pride follow, and their light fades. Today's word.
Your line: oh, the taste! A whole fall from light began with one finger. Day five hundred sixty, done.
